Linnaeus two-toed sloths (Choloepus didactylus) exhibit a suite of life-history traits that align closely with their famously slow metabolic pace. In captive colonies maintained at a steady core temperature of 33 °C [T = 33 °C], females attain sexual maturity after a prolonged developmental period, with puberty recorded at 1279 days since birth [tp = 1279 days since birth], a remarkably protracted interval reflecting the species’ low basal metabolic rate and delayed somatic growth. Males, in contrast, require an even longer pre-reproductive phase, reaching sexual maturity at 1644 days since birth [tp = 1644 days since birth] at a temperature of 33 °C [T = 33 °C]. This pronounced sexual dimorphism in maturation time is unusual among arboreal folivores and likely relates to the competitive demands of establishing a home range in the canopy. Gestation itself is correspondingly extended; under identical thermal conditions, pregnancy lasts a total of 279 days [tg = 279 days] at 33 °C [T = 33 °C]. Such a lengthy gestation period, approaching that of some primates of comparable body size, underscores the energetic constraints imposed by a diet of leaves with low nutrient density.

Neonatal Choloepus didactylus enter the world weighing just 410 grams [Wwb = 410 grams], a modest mass that is typical of the low metabolic rate of xenarthrans and represents only about 6.5% of the adult female mass. Female sloths ultimately reach an adult wet body mass of 6290 grams [Wwi = 6290 grams], a value that represents an approximately fifteen-fold increase from birth and places them among the larger-bodied folivores within the xenarthran clade. This substantial growth trajectory is supported by an extended period of maternal care. The time elapsed since birth at weaning has been documented at 152 days [tx = 152 days] under controlled captive conditions at 33 °C [T = 33 °C]. During this nursing interval, the dependent offspring remains in constant physical contact with the mother, a behavior that likely conserves energy and maintains thermal stability for the developing juvenile. The relatively protracted suckling stage, combined with the high degree of maternal investment, is a common pattern among tropical mammals with slow life histories.

The slow pace of life in Choloepus didactylus is further reflected in its maximum reproductive rate. This extremely low annual reproductive output, equating to fewer than 0.6 offspring per year, is among the lowest recorded for any mammal of its body size class. It aligns with the species’ reliance on a high-fiber diet that yields limited digestible energy, thereby constraining the resources available for gestation and lactation. The singular nature of each birth event means that every surviving offspring carries considerable demographic weight, rendering population growth acutely sensitive to any increase in juvenile mortality or disruption of the prolonged maternal care period.

Longevity data for Linnaeus two-toed sloths provide a consistent picture of a species operating on a slow time scale. Individuals maintained at a stable body temperature of 33 °C [T = 33 °C] have been documented to live up to roughly 31 years [am = up to roughly 31 years], a lifespan equivalent to approximately 11315 days that exceeds the maximum longevity reported for many similarly sized arboreal mammals. This extended lifespan is hypothesized to be a consequence of their exceptionally low mass-specific metabolic rate, which reduces cumulative oxidative damage over time. The ability to persist for over three decades in captivity suggests that wild individuals, while facing predation and disease, may nonetheless enjoy considerable longevity compared to other neotropical tree-dwellers. Such a long life, combined with the low annual fecundity and late age at first reproduction, classifies Choloepus didactylus as an archetypal slow life-history strategist, a pattern that appears tightly linked to its distinctive physiological profile.
